The 10-decision-equivalent resolution rule decides the abstract's last sentence without a sensitivity check
**Severity**: Minor
**Evidence Anchor**: text: §IV-C para. 3 "a resolution rule of our choosing"
**Confidence**: 3 — the timing is inferred from §IV-D; it is not clear whether phase-level values were among those already known

Location: §IV-C para. 3; Supplement S8.1; §IV-D bullet 4; Table S13(b).

Problem. The threshold was fixed in Amendment 05, when the class average's reaction-and-stop results were already known (§IV-D). At 6 m/s² the perfect oracle's frontier is zero, so den₀ equals the class average's summed frontier and its size could be anticipated. The abstract's final sentence follows from den₀ = 3.69 being below 10. At 4 m/s², however, the phase-weighted den₀ is 14.81 and the prior's share is 0.63, and under signed caution den₀ is 11.52. Evaluability is also judged on the point estimate of den₀, not on its interval.

Fix.
1. Report the branch the rule gives at other thresholds, for example 5 and 20 decision-equivalents.
2. As a sensitivity, base evaluability on den₀'s lower percentile limit.
3. Say in §IV-D whether the phase-level class-average frontiers under the reaction-and-stop scoring were among the values already known.

The symbols R and RR(N) mean different things in Table III and Fig. 4(b) than in the Notation table
**Severity**: Minor
**Evidence Anchor**: table: Table III, header columns R (pp) and RR(N), read against the Notation table rows for R and RR_E(A)
**Confidence**: 4 — read directly from the tables and captions

The Notation table defines R as the oracle's room under the 3 s commitment and RR_E(A) as a source's share of the 3 s oracle's advantage under another scoring. Table III (and Table S6) nevertheless heads that advantage under the reaction-and-stop scoring R, its caption calling it "the 3 s oracle's advantage", and heads the share RR(N); Fig. 4(b) labels its axis RR(N); Table IV calls the same share RR_E(N). Fix: relabel Table III, Table S6 and Fig. 4(b) with RR_E(N) and a distinct symbol for the 3 s oracle's advantage under the reaction-and-stop scoring, and use the same symbols in Section V-C.

Who bears the braking prior's costs is only partly named; comfort and following traffic are unmeasured
**Problem**: The "prior has costs" paragraph of §VI reports three things: lost progress (zero-margin caution of 1.72% against 1.10%), a scenario selection that favours the prior, and the untested case where braking never comes. It does not name two parties that pay for a planner that predicts braking for every moving lead with a nonzero acceleration estimate. Occupants pay through harder or more frequent early deceleration; caution measures how much speed is given up, not how. Vehicles behind the ego pay through rear-end exposure and car-following disturbances, which commercial adaptive cruise controllers already amplify (Gunter et al., below); the paper never mentions following traffic. The scope sentence of §I excludes other road users and scenarios but does not name them: pedestrians and cyclists, crossing and cut-in actors, vehicles behind the ego, and real sensor data.
**Why it matters**: §VII locates the measurable decision value in anticipating braking. A reader who weighs that value against its costs sees only the occupants' lost progress.
**Suggested fix**:
1. Name occupants' comfort and following traffic as unmeasured costs in the "prior has costs" paragraph and in §VI Limits.
2. As a comfort proxy that needs no new data, report for each arm, at matched caution, the distribution of the selected row's first target acceleration (the row labels of Table S7) or of its peak jerk.
3. In §I Scope, list the road users and scenarios left out.

**Severity**: Minor
**Evidence Anchor**: text: §VI "The prior has costs: its zero-margin caution is 1.72% against 1.10%" and "its cost where braking never comes is untested here"
**Confidence**: 4 — core expertise: how safety cases allocate residual risk

The closed-loop check's fallback share is missing where readers meet its sizing figures
**Problem**: The opening paragraph of S3 summarises the check as information-free planners needing about 0.31–0.35 s of starting gap beyond the legal following distance. Only the third paragraph of S3.4 reports two further facts. At the selected commitment times the planner was in its full-braking fallback in 0.70–0.72 of decisions, against 0.06 for Td. One scan step below those times there were 13 low-speed contacts. The Fig. S3 caption gives the contact counts but not the fallback share. §VI, where most readers meet the check, states its role and two of its limits correctly but gives neither fact.
**Why it matters**: Read alone, the opening paragraph looks like sizing guidance for a planner without covariance margins. A planner that sits in emergency fallback for most of a hard-braking episode is not a deployable design. A reader could therefore take away a much cheaper result than the check supports.
**Suggested fix**:
1. Add the fallback share and the contact count to the opening paragraph of S3, and the fallback share to the Fig. S3 caption.
2. Add one clause to the §VI sentence, for example "and its planners reach these gaps while in full-braking fallback in about 70% of decisions".
3. State explicitly that the gap figures are not design guidance.
4. S3 itself says the check does not test the paper's question; if it is not needed, consider removing it.

**Severity**: Minor
**Evidence Anchor**: text: Supplement S3 "at about 0.31–0.35 s of extra starting gap over the legal following distance"; S3.4 "The cost in starting gap therefore leaves out a large cost in comfort and progress."
**Confidence**: 4 — core expertise: interpreting closed-loop safety evidence

The margin propagates the tracker's covariance without process noise, and Section III-B does not say so

§III-B defines s = zᵀPz with z = (n, tₑn). This is the position–velocity posterior propagated at constant velocity, without the process-noise term of the prediction covariance (F P Fᵀ + Q in [35]). Table I describes N as the tracker's own logged covariance, projected. The omission of process noise is stated only in Supplement S9 and Table S14.

A domain reader will assume the planner uses the tracker's predicted covariance over the look-ahead. Q is fixed per class, so adding it would change N and F0 alike and push their ratio further towards 1; the null is unaffected. But F0's frontier, and with it the room and the priors' shares, are computed for a margin that grows only through the velocity block. The t⁴ terms of the Q and AM arms are the paper's only probes of an added growth term.

Fix:
- Say in §III-B and Table I that the margin is the posterior propagated without process noise.
- Give the reason (for example, the margin form of [9]).
- Note that a common class-level Q would leave the comparison of N with F0 unchanged.
- If feasible, report the room and RR(CK3) with F P Fᵀ + Q(tₑ) for F0.

**Severity**: Minor
**Evidence Anchor**: text: Supplement S9 "the planner's propagated deviation (no process noise) is too narrow on average by a factor of about 3.2"
**Confidence**: 4 — prediction-covariance propagation is standard estimation material.

4 Logic chain, hidden assumption; 7 Stakeholder blind spots

The comparison assumes that equal caution means equal cost, and the paper does not show this. Caution is the ego's mean speed loss averaged over truly safe selections only. Its sensitivity is untested for the 3 s shares, including the 83% and the 0.665. Where it was tested (τ = 0.75 s), counting caution at its signed value turned the prior's share negative with the ego moving (−0.90) and phase-weighted (−1.77, about 20 more wrong-go decisions). Caution also leaves out the braking that a margin induces, such as the fallback full-braking share and the commanded deceleration, whose cost falls on occupants and on vehicles behind the ego. No arm's braking demand is reported in the open-loop evaluation.

not norm-based

not norm-based

Recompute the 3 s shares (all decisions, ego moving, phase-weighted) with signed caution. At matched caution, report each arm's share of fallback full-braking selections and its mean and 95th-percentile commanded deceleration. If the signed-caution value of the 83% differs materially, replace it in the abstract; otherwise state in the abstract that it uses safe-selection caution.

**Evidence Anchor**: text: Section VI "The 3 s shares, including the 83% and the 0.665, count caution over truly safe selections only"; Section V-C "With the ego moving, however, it recovers less than the class average"

The headline question has an answer the paper itself calls expected
**Severity**: Major
**Evidence Anchor**: text: §I para. 4 "For a fixed-noise Kalman filter the covariance's null is expected"; §II Novelty "our contribution is to measure its decision consequence against an oracle with demonstrated room"
**Confidence**: 4 — editorial judgement of contribution framing, squarely within the handling editor's remit

Section I and the novelty paragraph of Section II state that the covariance's null follows from the steady state of a fixed-noise filter, yet the title poses exactly that question and contribution 2 presents its confirmation as a contribution. A screening editor will read the headline as a known result. What is new to an ITS reader is the evaluation design (equal caution, an oracle positive control, the graded-oracle check of Table S12, an explicit commitment model) and the finding that the open-loop room moves strongly with the commitment; these are under-sold. Fix: retitle around the question actually answered (a decision-level, equal-caution evaluation of tracker-covariance margins, with the fixed-noise tracker in lead braking as the case); reorder the contributions so the method and the commitment dependence come first and the covariance diagnostic third, introduced as a confirmatory test of an expected steady state; and add one sentence in Section I on why measuring an expected null was still needed (the covariance also depends on detections, misses and track age, as Section VI notes). This is rewriting, not new experiments. A stronger, costlier option is to apply the same evaluation to one source whose covariance does vary per decision (the calibrated covariance of [9], or an IMM tracker), which would show the method discriminating on a real tracker rather than only on synthetic graded oracles.

The recorded lead braking is milder than the assumed stop and the regulation's test, and the 12% headline does not say so
**Problem**: Recorded leads brake at 2.0–5.5 m/s² and none brakes harder (S2). The reaction-and-stop scoring assumes the ego stops at 6 m/s². The paper reports that R157's following test uses at least 6 m/s² for the lead (S3.2), and model 2 assumes 7 m/s² for the other vehicle. The commitment sensitivity is therefore measured only where the ego's assumed stop is at least as hard as anything the lead does. The paper's own sweep over stop decelerations (0.253 at 4 m/s² down to 0.064 at 7.6 m/s², §V-C) shows that the room is sensitive to this relation. The main text gives the lead's deceleration only as bins of the stopping-point error (§III-A), never as a condition on the scope.
**Why it matters**: Benchmark designers and assessors may read the Abstract's "with a perfect 6 m/s² stop 0.75 s after committing, it falls to 12%" as a general property of open-loop decision scores. The case in which a lead brakes harder than the ego's assumed stop, which both the regulation's test and model 2 include, is absent from the recordings.
**Suggested fix**:
1. State the 2.0–5.5 m/s² range in §III-A and §I Scope.
2. Qualify the 12% and the 53% in §V-C, §VI and, if space allows, the Abstract with "for leads braking at up to 5.5 m/s²".
3. Add to §VI Limits that the closed-loop check (leads at 6–7 m/s²) and the open-loop runs cover different braking severities.
4. Name harder lead braking as future work; it needs new recordings.

**Severity**: Minor
**Evidence Anchor**: text: Supplement S2 "No recording brakes above 5.5 m/s²."; Supplement S3.2 "the regulation's following test uses at least 6 m/s²"
**Confidence**: 3 — adjacent expertise: scenario-based validation; the link between lead and ego decelerations is my reading, not something the paper shows

Paper-specific terms are used before definition, and names drift
**Severity**: Minor
**Evidence Anchor**: text: §I contribution 3 "Against a perfect oracle for that scoring, the phase-weighted avoidable wrong-go is 6% of the pooled amount"; §V-C "the inflated covariance 0.012"
**Confidence**: 4 — read directly from the text

Section I and the contribution list use room, caution, commitment, phase-weighted, avoidable wrong-go and "a perfect oracle" before Section IV defines them, and the Notation table arrives only after Section IV-C. Names drift for one object: the NA arm is the NIS-inflated covariance, an innovation-inflated variant or the inflated covariance; CK3 is the braking prior, a braking prediction or a constant-deceleration braking prediction; F0 is the class average, the class-average covariance or the class-average margin. Fix: give one-sentence plain definitions of room, caution and the two commitment models in Section I; move the Notation table to the start of Section IV and add the arm codes to it; after Section III-C use one name per arm consistently in text, tables and figures.

The title asks, as an open question, something that filter theory already answers for the tracker tested

The tracker tested is a single-model linear Kalman filter with fixed class-level noise and updates at about 2 Hz. For such a filter the covariance does not depend on the data and converges to the Riccati steady state ([35], [36]; §II). Its near-constancy, and therefore a null at equal caution, is predicted before any run, and the paper says so (§I, §II "Novelty, with its limits", §VI). What the evaluation adds beyond theory is the room, the priors' shares and the commitment dependence.

The title and the Abstract's first sentence still pose the general question for "a Kalman tracker". The untested cases (IMM, adaptive noise, a calibrated covariance, range-dependent measurement noise) are exactly those where theory does not settle the answer.

Fix (minimum): qualify the title, for example "a Fixed-Noise Kalman Tracker's Covariance". Add one Abstract sentence saying that the null is the steady-state expectation and that the measured contribution is the room and its location.

Fix (stronger): compute the steady-state covariance of the tracker's vehicle-class model at the update interval, and the margin ratio it implies. Then show that the 1.10 of Fig. 2(b) and its 0.74% tail follow from it plus re-initialisations and missed detections. This turns contribution 2 into a quantitative check of the theory.

The null's practical relevance would also be stronger if the paper showed how common fixed-noise Kalman trackers are in automated-driving perception. Examples are AB3DMOT (Weng, Wang, Held and Kitani, 2020) and the probabilistic tracker of Chiu, Prioletti, Li and Bohg (2020), which sets its noise terms from training-set statistics.

**Severity**: Minor
**Evidence Anchor**: text: Title "Does a Kalman Tracker's Covariance Improve Car-Following Decisions?"
**Confidence**: 4 — Kalman steady-state behaviour and the tracking practice of the field are within my competence.

The NIS-inflated arm tests only the covariance channel of adaptive filtering

§II places NA in the line of covariance matching and adjustable-level process noise, and §V-B is headed as a test of an adaptive covariance. In covariance matching [32], [33] and in adjustable-level process noise [35, Sec. 11.2], the noise estimate enters the filter. At a manoeuvre this raises the gain and reduces the lag of the state estimate. NA instead scales only the output covariance and leaves the state estimate unchanged.

That lag is present in these runs: the mean error is −0.29 [−0.35, −0.22] m at t = 0 while the lead brakes (§V-D). The way an adaptive filter would most plausibly change decisions in lead braking is therefore outside this arm. The paper states the inflate-only limitation and that the covariance is too wide (median per-run mean NIS 0.24). However, its paragraph "What an adaptive covariance would need" (§VI) discusses only the direction in which the covariance adapts.

Fix:
- Retitle §V-B, for example "An NIS-scaled output covariance and simple priors".
- State in §II and §VI that NA isolates the covariance channel and does not test the gain or state-estimate effect of adaptive filtering.
- List that effect with IMM among the untested cases.

**Severity**: Minor
**Evidence Anchor**: text: §V-B heading "An Adaptive Covariance and Simple Priors"
**Confidence**: 4 — adaptive and manoeuvring-target filtering is within my competence.

The room and every commitment ratio are defined only for contact, not for the 2 m standstill gap of the regulatory model the paper adopts

A decision is a wrong go when the selected row's true clearance reaches zero (§IV-A). The reaction-and-stop scoring is reported at zero standstill gap (Table III, Fig. 4).

The paper takes τ, A and the jerk from performance model 2 of the 01 series of R157 [39]. The same parameter set contains a 2 m safety distance at complete stop. The paper itself uses that distance as d_stop = 2 m in Supplement S3.1 and as the 2 m line of its closed-loop results (S3.4).

With a 2 m gap, the 3 s oracle stops being an oracle. The 3 s scoring's summed frontier difference becomes negative (footnote to Table S6). The reaction-and-stop room at τ = 0.75 s is −0.10 [−1.89, 1.29] points (Table S6), and no ratio is interpreted.

So the 5.56-point room, the 12% and 53% of the Abstract, and the location of the room under the reaction-and-stop scoring all hold for contact only. Neither the Abstract nor the Limits paragraph states this criterion. The covariance null is not affected: at 2 m, Table S1 gives D(N, F0)/201 between −0.0147 and +0.0028 points.

Fix (minimum): state in the Abstract's commitment sentence and in Limits that a wrong go means contact (zero standstill gap), and that at the regulatory 2 m gap the oracle-based room is undefined.

Fix (stronger): score the perfect oracle O of §IV-C, which the paper already builds for every zero-gap scoring, at a 2 m gap under both the 3 s scoring and the τ = 0.75 s scoring. Report den₀, RR₀(N) and RR₀(CK3) there, so that the claims about commitment dependence and the room's location can be read at the gap the cited regulation uses.

Field-norm basis: the 2 m safety distance at complete stop in [39, Annex 3, Table 3], as the authors cite it in S3.1.

**Severity**: Major
**Evidence Anchor**: text: Supplement S5, footnote to Table S6, "the 3 s oracle is not an oracle"
**Confidence**: 3 — the manuscript does not compute a perfect oracle at a 2 m gap, so how much the results would change is uncertain.

Overlap with the author's related manuscript and reliance on unrefereed preprints need managing
**Severity**: Minor
**Evidence Anchor**: text: §I Scope "A related manuscript by the author [9], under review, asks how to size a margin from a tracker's covariance"
**Confidence**: 4 — standard editorial handling of related submissions and preprint citations

The related manuscript [9], under review at IEEE Access, shares the detector architecture, the tracker configuration and the margin form; Section I discloses this and states that no data, result or figure of [9] is used. The editor will still need [9] to judge overlap. Positioning also rests partly on 2026 preprints: the tracker itself [8] (arXiv, noted as accepted to IROS 2026) and [14], [17] and [19]. Fix: upload [9] as a confidential related manuscript and state in the cover letter what is shared and what is new; cite the IROS proceedings version of [8] if it is available; check [14], [17] and [19] for published versions; make sure no positioning sentence rests on a preprint alone.

The 2 Hz update rate, which sets the state's age, is neither justified nor listed as a limit

The tracker updates the lead at about 2 Hz, and decisions use states 0–0.4 s old (§III-A, §V-D). §V-D shows that the ranking of the error comes from the state's age, and the lag behind a braking lead grows with that age. The update rate therefore shapes the error while the lead brakes, and part of the room.

The manuscript gives no reason for 2 Hz, for example inheritance from the configuration of [9] or a keyframe rate, and the Limits paragraph does not mention it. The covariance null does not depend on the rate, because a steady state exists at any regular interval.

Fix:
- State where the 2 Hz rate comes from, add it to Limits, and scope the §V-D ranking result and the lead-braking room to it.
- If the recordings hold sensor frames at a higher rate, rerun the tracker at that rate on the evaluation runs. This would show how much of the lead-braking room is lag due to the state's age.

**Severity**: Minor
**Evidence Anchor**: text: §III-A "the tracker updates the lead at about 2 Hz (68 updates in a full-length run)"
**Confidence**: 3 — this is an inference from the paper's own evidence; the rate's origin may be documented in [9], which I have not seen.

Caution, the axis of every frontier, conditions on the outcome, and the headline 3 s shares were never rerun with the unconditioned definition
**Severity**: Major
**Evidence Anchor**: text: §IV-A "Decisions whose selected row is unsafe do not enter this average" and §VI Limits "count caution over truly safe selections only, and their sensitivity to that choice is untested"
**Confidence**: 4 — the selection effect follows from the definition; its size at the 3 s commitment is unknown until it is computed

Location: §IV-A; §V-C para. 4; Table S13(a); §VI Limits.

Problem. Caution is averaged only over decisions whose selected row is truly safe. Each arm's caution is therefore computed on a different subset of decisions, selected by the outcome, so arms with different wrong-go rates are compared at "equal caution" measured over different denominators. The paper ran the obvious alternative (the signed speed difference to the 3 s oracle's row, over all decisions) only at τ = 0.75 s. There it reversed the braking prior's sign with the ego moving (from 0.034 to −0.90 [−1.47, −0.49]) and in the phase-weighted aggregate (to −1.77 [−3.27, −1.12]), and it lowered the pooled share from 0.936 to 0.80. The 3 s results that carry the abstract and the conclusion were not rerun: the 83% [75%, 90%], the 0.665 phase-weighted share, the 0.61 while the lead brakes, and the acceleration margin's 38%.

Why it matters. The conclusion "the decision value we could measure lies in anticipating braking under the 3 s commitment" rests on the 3 s shares. The only evidence on this design choice shows that it can flip signs, in exactly the populations where the measure is weakest.

Fix.
1. Rerun the 3 s scoring with caution counted over all evaluated decisions (signed), for every arm and every population of Table S5, using the existing signed-caution code (two programs already exist).
2. Print the results beside Table II. Revise the abstract's 83% sentence and the conclusion if the ego-moving or phase-weighted value changes sign or branch.
3. In future plans, prefer a caution definition that does not condition on the safety outcome.

1 Core thesis; 6 Alternative paths

The positive control sizes a room that a covariance may not be able to use. So "at most about 0.4% of the room", and its contrast with the prior's 83%, are not like-for-like. The oracle sets each constraint's margin from the realised error, which is close to the true safety label (R is 5.6 of the 6.0-point mean height of F0's frontier). Dividing each decision's oracle critical values by a log-normal factor with σ = 2 scrambles the per-decision scale but keeps the within-decision pattern, and it still leaves 0.82 of the room pooled. The room therefore lies mainly in where along each row the realised error exceeds the clearance. A covariance can change that pattern only through the shared projection z = (n, t_e n). Its main lever is the per-decision scale, and the room open to that scale is never measured. The CK3 contrast sets a mean-path correction, which changes the pattern, against variance scalings.

not norm-based

not norm-based

Add a positive control in the covariance's own form: per decision, the position–velocity covariance (or a multiple of the class-average covariance) fitted to that decision's realised error over the 3 s window and projected exactly as N. Report its room, and RR(N) and RR(NA) against it, beside the current R. If that room is small, say the covariance had little to recover; if it is large, the null gains force. Rephrase the CK3-versus-covariance sentences as a contrast between a mean-path correction and variance margins.

**Evidence Anchor**: table: Table S12, rows "Noisy, σ = 1" and "Noisy, σ = 2", column "3 s, all: RR" (0.922 and 0.820)

Percentile intervals for ratios whose denominators approach zero are unstable
**Severity**: Minor
**Evidence Anchor**: table: Table S10, count (ii), τ = 0.75 s, lead-braking row (RR₀(CK3) 0.266 [0.098, 1.237]; den₀ 45.00 [6.18, 72.22]; 1.57% of resamples at or below zero)
**Confidence**: 4 — standard behaviour of ratio estimators

Location: Tables S9–S10; §V-C para. 5.

Problem. While the lead brakes under count (ii), the braking prior's share is printed as 0.27 [0.10, 1.24]. Resamples with den₀ at or below zero (1.57%) are dropped before the percentile is taken. An upper limit above 1, for a share of a perfect oracle's avoidable wrong-go, reflects resamples in which the denominator nearly vanishes. Dropping up to 2.5% of resamples also conditions the interval on the denominator. The same pattern recurs in Tables S9–S10 (for example RR₀(E) [0.225, 2.056] in the same row).

Fix. Where den₀'s interval approaches zero, report D and den₀ with their joint interval (partly given already in decision-equivalents) or a Fieller-type interval for the ratio, and flag such cells instead of printing a percentile interval for the ratio.

The braking prior is labelled RSS-style and reported at a single deceleration that matches the scenarios

The braking prior CK3 shifts each tracked actor's predicted path as if it braked at 3 m/s², whenever its acceleration estimate is nonzero and it moves faster than 0.5 m/s (§III-C, Table I). Section VI calls this an RSS-style assumption and reads the 83% as the share that "an RSS-style fixed braking prior captures".

RSS [37] is a worst-case envelope. Its safe longitudinal distance assumes, unconditionally, that the front vehicle brakes at its maximum deceleration and that the rear vehicle responds only after a response time. CK3 is something else: a nominal mean prediction from the physics-based constant-acceleration family, at a moderate deceleration, combined with F0's variance. The paper also uses the RSS label for two different objects: CK3 at 3 m/s², and the worst-case stopping rule of Supplement S3.1 at b_o = 7 m/s² ("of the RSS form [37]").

The value 3 m/s² lies inside the leads' own braking range in these recordings (2.0–5.5 m/s², Supplement S2). The manuscript does not say how 3 m/s² was chosen. Only the prior's timing and stop clip are varied, which moves its share between 0.72 and 0.83 (§V-B, §VI). The 83% appears in the Abstract, contribution 3, §VI and the Conclusion. As reported, it is the share captured by a deceleration that matches the scenario family, not by an RSS-type worst-case assumption.

Fix (minimum):
- Rename CK3 a constant-deceleration prediction, and remove "RSS-style" from §II, §VI and the Conclusion; keep the RSS label for the S3 rule.
- Place CK3 among physics-based motion models, for example the constant-velocity and constant-acceleration families reviewed by Lefèvre, Vasquez and Laugier (2014).
- State how 3 m/s² was chosen on the tuning runs.
- Add to Limits that this value lies inside the evaluation runs' braking range.

Fix (stronger): report RR(CK3) over a sweep of the assumed deceleration, for example 2, 4, 6 and 7 m/s². The paper already takes 7 m/s², the other vehicle's maximum deceleration, from [39] in S3. Readers could then see how much of the 83% survives a deceleration that does not match the scenarios.

Field-norm basis: the definition of RSS's longitudinal rule in [37], which the authors cite.

**Severity**: Major
**Evidence Anchor**: text: §VI "a fixed 3 m/s² braking prediction, an RSS-style assumption [37], captures 83% of the pooled room"
**Confidence**: 4 — RSS and constant-deceleration prediction are core to my area; I have not seen how the tuning runs led to 3 m/s².

Number formats and precision are inconsistent
**Severity**: Minor
**Evidence Anchor**: table: Table II, row RR(N)
**Confidence**: 4 — read directly from the text and tables

Shares appear as percentages in the Abstract and Section I (0.7 to 2.5%, 83%) and as decimals with three to six significant figures in the body and tables (0.0167 [0.00729, 0.0252]; −0.000131 [−0.00577, 0.00159] in Table II), and the braking prior's share is printed as 0.8315, 0.831 and 83%. Fix: one convention, for example percentages with two significant figures in prose and decimals with three significant figures in tables, with intervals rounded to the precision the bootstrap supports.

The operating domain of the recordings, and of the borrowed R157 values, is not stated
**Problem**: UN R157 and its 01 series [38], [39] apply to ALKS on roads where pedestrians and cyclists are prohibited and opposing traffic is physically separated, and their performance models were set for that domain. The manuscript states neither the road type or setting of the CARLA recordings (desired speeds 5–15 m/s, most decisions at standstill behind a stopped lead) nor that it borrows the regulation's values as reference parameters outside the regulation's scope.
**Why it matters**: Before giving the τ = 0.75 s results any weight, an assessor will want to know whether the regulatory parameters are applied inside or outside the domain they were set for.
**Suggested fix**:
1. In §III-A, give the road type and setting of the recordings.
2. In §IV-C, add that the R157 values serve as reference parameters, not as a claim about ALKS or about compliance.

**Severity**: Minor
**Evidence Anchor**: absence: §III-A and §IV-C — expected the road type and operating domain of the CARLA recordings and a statement that the R157 values are borrowed outside the regulation's motorway scope; checked §I Scope, §III-A, §IV-C, §VI Limits, Supplement S3.1, S3.2 and S8.1
**Confidence**: 3 — adjacent expertise: R157 scope; I am confident of the regulation's road-type scope but cannot tell from the text where the runs were recorded

4 Logic chain; 5 Overgeneralization

The prior's decision value is measured off-policy. Every decision state was produced by a planner whose margin used the tracker's covariance, so CK3 is scored on states its own planner would not visit. Most of those states come after the stop (82.7%), where CK3 recovers 0.99 of that phase's room. The commitment analysis varies what follows a decision but not which states the decisions are taken in, and the closed-loop check never runs the prior. For CK3, "decision value" is therefore an open-loop, off-policy quantity.

Open-loop scores can diverge from closed-loop driving quality: [26] Codevilla et al., ECCV 2018, and [27] Dauner et al., CoRL 2023, both cited in Section II

The paper's remedy, commitment sensitivity, covers the consequence horizon but not the state distribution.
